newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr recoups losses but risks remain.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr recoups losses but risks remain.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished a thin Thursday session with 1/3 cent of gains and a modest upward momentum courtesy of U.S. shortcovering.

Traders said U.S. bankd and funds that had sold earlier in the week had to reverse themselves after the Federal Reserve declined to raise U.S. interest rates and investors rediscovered their liking for higher yielding currencies.

The resulting rally recaptured 79 cents and recouped all the losses suffered in Tuesday's slump to a US$0.7855 one-month low. Further gains would be hard to come by, however, given the lingering risk of a reduction in domestic rates before year end.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar had hiked to US$0.7916/21, the day's high, from an early US$0.7905/10 and Wednesday's late US$0.7880/85.

A break of resistance at US$0.945, last week's peak, was needed to inject life into the old uptrend, while a breach of US$0.7855 support would suggest the recent correction had further to run and a test of the pivotal US$0.7810 was coming.

The currency was up sharply on the crosses, aided by a strong U.S. dollar and a switch toward high yielders, at 87.44/54 yen and 1.2001/16 marks from 86.40/50 and 1.1867/79 Wednesday. In trade weighted terms it rose to 58.3 from 58.0.

Traders said the Fed's inaction had attracted a flood of offfshore funds into U.S. Treasuries, so boosting the U.S. dollar in the process. The local currency, as a perceived member of the dollar bloc, hitched a ride on the bullish bandwagon.

The exodus from the yen and mark was given added impetus by increasing confidence that European Monetary Union would take place which made the higher yielding European currencies, and particularly the Italian lira, seem a safer bet.
The Australian dollar's status as a high yielder was somewhat in doubt, however, given that many analysts looked for another cut in domestic rates in the next few months.

Some even saw a chance the Reserve Bank would ease policy as soon as next week following its monthly board meeting on Tuesday. Most considered this a long shot but conceded the Fed's inaction had slightly raised the risk by helping to take pressure off the local dollar.
That risk had not been priced into the dollar as yet, so dealers expected nerves to build into next week.

Today's trickle of domestic data added to the impression of a soft labour market which might well need another boost from easier monetary policy to stir the sort of jobs growth needed to reduce the unemployment rate.
National job vacancies for the August quarter were reported to have fallen 1.2 percent after a 7.5 percent fall the previous quarter.

This was not quite as weak as analysts had feared, however, and vacancies in the private sector actually rose 2.6 percent while all the losses were in the public sector, where the government has been busy cutting employment as part of its budget tightening plans.
But a seperate release showed skilled job vacancies eased 0.7 percent in September, suggesting the labour market was drifting sideways into the fourth quarter.
The other main driving force behind the local dollar was trends in world commodity prices, and here too the omens were not particularly bullish for the medium term.
The influential Commodity Research Bureau index of futures contracts had bounced 3.28 points in the last couple of days but at 247.12 remained far below its April high of 263.79.
Above trend U.S. growth and economic recoveries in Japan and Europe had the potential to boost commodity demand and prices but probably not until 1997, analsyts added.
